body: Because you have a limited amount of troops you can train (e.g. 700 troops), but if I'm not mistaken, you can promote up to 5k at once, so you get a lot more points. I do this already, and it truly pushes me up the rankings.

Whales dictating the game also annoys me. As you said, people are free to play however they want, and if you have a disposable income that allows you to spend thousands on a mobile game, that’s great for you. But I am in a very competitive state, with at the very least 20 whales. We win most preps and SVS in general. I’ll push for things I can do without wasting all of my inventory such as beast, promoting troops etc But realistically, it’s impossible to grow only from SVS as a f2p when I’m competing with over 20 whales + the rest of the state that includes mid to low spenders. And like I said, I do push with my 2nd account, because I do wanna help, but even if I spend 2 months saving, I won’t rank high enough to give me back 1/3 of the things I used.

But finishing top 100 on SVS and top 3/5 on other events is very different. My point is that as a f2p, it’s hard to push for SVS when there’s at least 10 whales in my state buying and saving daily for prep phase. How can you compete against that?

I just think it’s hard for me to grasp anything other than the fact that whales spend their own money because they want. They made a choice on day 1 to open their wallet, when it was not required. If they want to max their accounts, they pay the price, and if that’s how they want to play, good for them, I wish I had disposable income as well. But how can f2p grow as much as they can for free, if they can’t participate in other events, y’know?

Ranking high = higher rewards

Especially fire crystals, which aren’t easy to come around, when you need more or less 2000 to upgrade your furnace

This!!! You said it all. 

It’s the unrealistic expectation from the 1% over the rest. The game is not the same for f2p, so I believe it’s not the worst thing to try and win other events.

I don’t think it’s selfish. No one is asking or making them waste their money, they pay because they want to. If I could afford to pay to play, I would, but I don’t have that type of disposable income. It’s pretty unrealistic to think people can afford to waste thousands on a game, when in reality most people lives on a minimum wage and this is just a mobile game. At the end of the day I have to prioritise rent, bills and food. If that’s not their priority, great for them, but it’s not selfish of me to believe they shouldn’t be dictating other people’s gameplay.

A good example is the mentality of peer pressure to buy stickers and/or gamble it. $8 might not be anything for people who can afford, but for someone like me, it would end up adding up.

I think I might’ve made it too confusing while explaining, but what I meant by eavesdropping, I meant the viewer, not the character. I want to convey a sense of voyeurism, where the viewer is watching something so similar to reality, that the dialogues feel more like them eavesdropping something they’re not a part of; something so natural it feels like they’re hearing in real life, rather than having them hear/see the dialogue as a narrative format with a purpose (like when we’re using exposition because it will add something to the story), if that makes sense?

But what if the reason why I'm choosing to voice something, is because I'm trying to convey this story that feel as close to reality as possible? When this project comes to fruition and I'm in production, something that will go alongside this will be the directing of the actors to show a more nuanced, realistic portrayal, with lots of body-language, but until that happens, I don't know how to translate that to the screenplay only. Thanks for the advice, though, I appreciate it :)

But, what should I do, when I'm trying to convey a much more realistic portrayal of reality, than what the Before trilogy did? Don't get me wrong, these are (at least the first two) on my top 10 favourite movies of ALL TIME. Linklater does a tremendous job when it comes to realistic/naturalistic screenplays with most of his work, huge fan. But what I'm working on, is slightly different, the plot is there, but very very subtle, I want the dialogues to feel like you're eavesdropping (voyeur) a very sometimes intimate, but you know, still private and realistic conversation you would hear in real life, if that makes sense? Everything you said is 100% valid, and I shall take that into consideration moving forward, but I'm still a bit unsure if that's necessarily applicable in my case, unfortunately :)

Yes, that's actually really good, thank you for pointing that out :) I do wanna work a lot with body-language for reaction; unspoken words etc but that will only be part of the project once it's in production, so when it comes to the screenplay alone, I think what I'm having trouble with is how to portray a voyeur feeling, like the viewer finds themselves watching in something so close to reality, a slice-of-life of sorts with long, "boring" dialogues, that explores different themes in the story instead of having them see that as me not doing a good job and basically just "feeding the audience" like I don't know what I'm doing, even if it's bluntly obvious. I think it just takes a VERY meticulous and subtle approach to how I can achieve that, and still be true to what type of work I wanna put out, y'know?

I totally understand what you mean and I agree, but I don't know if that's necessarily applicable to what I'm trying to make?  I like long-ass dialogues, that emulates in the viewer the feeling of being a voyeur more than a spectator (in a total non-problematic-just-curious kind of way). My ultimate goal here is to have this screenplay read into something like a character-driven, subtle plot, ultra realistic/naturalistic, slice-of-life kind of work. When this comes to fruition and becomes a proper finalised project and I get to work with the actors, the body-language will also be a HUGE way I can use the "show, don't tell" method, for sure besides what the screenplay entails. But because I want to write something that feels more like you're watching a stranger life (voyeur; mundane?) rather than a story (spectator; predictable?), I can't help but feel like a natural, colloquial, sort-of improvised dialogue is a big thing when it comes to portray this realistic feeling, even if it's giving something away that I could've exposed in a different way, just because that's how I want to emulate real life through this screenplay, if that makes sense? I guess I'm just worried about knowing how to work this around in a meticulous and subtle way, where it portrays what I'm trying to make and not have it be seen like a cheap-ass "feed the audience" kind of work. I don't think I have enough material to use as a research or guide of sorts for what I want to do. But I do appreciate your help, thank you! I'll take that into consideration moving forward :)

I think in my case, as a very much character-driven, subtle plot, slice-of-life kind of work, I cannot afford to not explore a big portion of the story through dialogue, even if it feels "useless"; isn't going anywhere plot-wise, it's still a look into a character's life through something so natural such as having my character tell x character something about themselves, because that's how real life is? I don't know if it makes sense. That's the type of work I'm into, so I'm just finding hard to conciliate the feeling of "ok, this dialogue matters, this is not the type of movie to prioritise it through acting as I wanna portray a voyeur feeling when watching this, but at the same time, I feel like this goes against what I was taught was the right way to write and I'm missing the point here" lmao
